{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=distinction+between+thermodynamic+persistence+and+heritable+information+storage+in+prebiotic+chemical+networks&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-3-319-53512-8_6\", \"title\": [\"Exchange of Information During Prebiotic Evolution\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-53512-8_6\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2017]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6493658\", \"title\": [\"Distinction Thermodynamic Economics (DTE): A Unified Theory of Economic Phenomena from Information-Theoretic First Principles\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>We propose Distinction Thermodynamic Economics (DTE), a theory that derives the core structures of economics-markets, firms, money, credit, financial crises, and macroeconomic aggregates-from a single primitive: the distinction, defined as a partition of the state space. Five axioms (self-maintaining agent, distinction primitive, finite budget, dissipation floor, power-weighted institutions) generate a three-layer cost function spanning physics (Landauer erasure), cognition (MDL complexity), and social verification/enforcement. From this base we derive: (i) a four-component decomposition of the interest rate into time-degradation, assessment, enforcement, and distinction-uncertainty premia; (ii) money as an optimal rate-distortion compression of multi-dimensional distinctions; (iii) an optimal coarse-graining problem (C⋆) whose fixed points are macroeconomic aggregates (GDP, price level, unemployment) and whose discontinuous jumps constitute a unified taxonomy of phase transitions-financial crises, technological revolutions, institutional transformations, and inflation; (iv) a value function grounded in future distinction-cost reduction; (v) prices as Lagrange multipliers on joint distinction-cost constraints, dissolving the subjective/objective value dichotomy. Existing theories emerge as classical limits: Arrow-Debreu (Γ → 0, B → ∞), rational inattention (DTE minus the social layer), behavioural biases (budget-optimal heuristics), Coase (Σ market vs. Σ firm), Akerlof (distinction-cost critical point), Modigliani-Miller (Γ → 0), Diamond-Dybvig (processing-capacity bottleneck), and Minsky (endogenous λ-accumulation). Six pre-registered empirical tests-targeting the distinction-complexity premium in bond spreads, the leading-indicator power of distinction leverage λ(t), relativeprice entropy as an inflation precursor, complexity×capacity interaction in behavioural biases, the securitisation distinction gap, and power-weighted institutional selection-provide sharp rejection conditions. Full identification strategies (DID, RD, event study) and a structural-estimation roadmap are specified.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6493658\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6487385\", \"title\": [\"Persistence-Driven Selection Before Replication Stabilization-Driven Differential Persistence as a Prebiotic Mechanism\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Selection is typically understood as a process operating on replicating entities, where differences in replication rates determine evolutionary outcomes. However, the emergence of such replicators remains a central unresolved problem in prebiotic evolution. Here, we propose that selection can occur prior to replication through differential persistence of molecular structures. We define selection as the differential persistence of molecular structures under environmental constraints, and show that such persistence differences can arise from environment-dependent stabilization driven by physicochemical interactions. In this framework, environmental conditions induce stabilization biases among molecular configurations, leading to measurable differences in survival time, persistence probability, or reaction lifetime. These differences constitute selection without requiring replication or heredity. This perspective establishes a pre-replicative regime of selection based on persistence, providing a mechanistic bridge between abiotic chemistry and later replication-based evolutionary dynamics. It complements existing frameworks including RNA world, autocatalytic sets, dissipative adaptation, and dynamic kinetic stability by explicitly formalizing selection in terms of differential persistence at the molecular level.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6487385\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1515/jnet-2022-0044\", \"title\": [\"Are all chemical reactions in principle reversible? Thermodynamic distinction between “conceptually complete” and “practically complete” reactions\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>\\n               <jats:p>Among the chemical reactions having a pronounced thermodynamic driving force to the formation of products, a distinction has to be made between processes which attain a chemical equilibrium state very much shifted towards the products and those where the final equilibrium state corresponds to the truly complete consumption of reactant(s), i.e. where a true chemical equilibrium is actually not attained under the given conditions. Based on a few selected examples, two thermodynamic arguments are led which rationalise the above distinction from different points of view: a phase-rule point of view and a Gibbs energy minimization approach. “Conceptually complete” reactions involve pure phases and, as a consequence, establishing chemical equilibrium would imply a negative variance, what is avoided by the complete consumption of one or more phases. In the Gibbs energy approach, “conceptually complete” reactions and “practically complete” ones can be distinguished (at fixed temperature and pressure) by the different way to attain the minimum Gibbs energy condition, respectively with sharp (not differentiable) and flat (zero derivative) minimum points as a function of the extent of reaction <jats:italic>ξ</jats:italic>.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1515/jnet-2022-0044\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2022, 12, 13]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "932ca9386f8affc65d17317e5082967cf78cb5d49078edb27086b39daf83c0c2", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "chemical_heredity", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.1007/978-3-319-53512-8_6", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6493658", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6487385", "doi:10.1515/jnet-2022-0044"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-53512-8_6", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6493658", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6487385", "https://doi.org/10.1515/jnet-2022-0044"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
